title: Why Did the Bronze Age Collapse?
creator: Edmund Hale
description:
Around 1177 BC, nearly every great civilization of the eastern Mediterranean fell within a few decades. What happened?

Chapters:
0:00 A world of kings
1:00 The Sea Peoples
1:50 Drought and earthquakes
2:40 The trade network
4:30 What came after

Sources in the pinned comment.

sentences.t: Around twelve hundred BC, the eastern Mediterranean was home to one of the most connected worlds in ancient history.
You had the Egyptians, the Hittites in what's now Turkey, the Mycenaean Greeks, the Babylonians, and rich trading cities like Ugarit on the Syrian coast.
Their kings wrote letters to each other, called each other brother, and swapped gold, horses, and the occasional princess.
And then, within maybe fifty years, almost all of it was gone.
Palaces burned, cities were abandoned, writing disappeared in Greece for centuries.
So what on earth happened?
The oldest explanation points at a group the Egyptians called the Sea Peoples.
Ramesses the Third left a huge inscription at Medinet Habu describing how they swept through land after land, and how he, of course, heroically defeated them.
We even have a heartbreaking letter from the last king of Ugarit, saying enemy ships have come and his own troops are away.
The tablet may never have been sent, because the city fell around then.
But for a long time, historians have been uneasy blaming everything on mysterious raiders.
Who were they, and why were they on the move in the first place?
That's where the climate comes in.
Pollen in lake sediments and other records suggest a long stretch of drought across the region around this time.
There are letters about grain shortages, with the Hittites begging Egypt for shipments of wheat.
On top of that, some archaeologists argue for a series of earthquakes rolling through the region over several decades.
Now, none of those things alone would bring down a whole world.
But together, they hit a system that was incredibly dependent on trade.
Bronze is copper plus tin, and almost nobody had both.
Copper came from places like Cyprus, and tin came from very far away, possibly as far as Central Asia.
So when trade routes broke, you didn't just lose luxuries, you lost the metal for weapons and tools.
Historians call this systems collapse, where each shock makes the next one worse, until the whole network fails at once.

So, what came after the collapse?
In Greece, a long period that used to be called the Dark Ages, with smaller villages and no writing for a few hundred years.
The Hittite empire vanished entirely, and Egypt survived, but it was never quite as powerful again.
But collapse is also a beginning.
Iron, which you could find almost anywhere, slowly replaced bronze, so you didn't need long trade routes anymore.
On the coast of the Levant, the Phoenicians spread an alphabet that the Greeks would later adopt.
So in a way, the collapse helped make the world of classical Greece possible.
